findings.claim: Avoid single-sided answers; the 2024 examiners' report flagged this as the most common reason for low scores on impacts questions.
findings.truth: No such examiners' report finding is cited or citable. The spec prints no question ladder and no report is named. This is a fabricated examiner claim and must go.
findings.evidence: spec section 11 (Impacts of digital technology on wider society) and spec 3.1; no examiners' report referenced anywhere in the source material

findings.claim: Examiners consistently penalise answers that list benefits in one paragraph and drawbacks in another without weighing them.
findings.truth: An unsourced claim about examiner behaviour. The point is sound as advice, so state it as a property of a weak answer, not as a claim about what examiners do.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1 (AO3: make reasoned judgements); no published examiner statement supports the wording

findings.claim: is what separates a Mastering response from a Secure one
findings.truth: House band vocabulary is Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band. The same lesson already says 'a top-band answer' earlier, so the prose is also internally inconsistent.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md copyright-distancing rule; lesson 1 paragraph n12

findings.claim: data centres account for around 1% of global electricity consumption (repeated in the key fact, in the conclusion, and in flashcard 6)
findings.truth: The IEA figure for 2024 is about 415 TWh, around 1.5% of global electricity consumption. 'Around 1%' understates the current value by roughly a third.
findings.evidence: IEA 2024 data-centre electricity figure via Wikipedia, Environmental impact of artificial intelligence

findings.claim: Unauthorised access to computer material ... This is a summary offence, punishable by up to 2 years in prison.
findings.truth: Section 1 of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 is triable either way, not summary only. The two-year maximum applies on conviction on indictment. The sentence is also self-contradictory: a summary offence cannot carry two years in a magistrates' court.
findings.evidence: legislation.gov.uk, Computer Misuse Act 1990 s1(3): 'on conviction on indictment, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years'

findings.claim: It implements the requirements of the UK GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) into domestic law following Brexit.
findings.truth: The Data Protection Act 2018 received Royal Assent on 23 May 2018, before the UK left the EU. It could not have been passed to implement the UK GDPR after Brexit. The UK GDPR is the retained version of the EU rules, created by the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018; the DPA 2018 sits alongside it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Data Protection Act 2018 (Royal Assent 23 May 2018; complements the GDPR; UK GDPR retained via the EU Withdrawal Act)

findings.claim: "Non-Commercial" (CC NC) restricts reuse to non-commercial purposes.
findings.truth: There is no Creative Commons licence called 'CC NC'. NonCommercial is a licence element, and every current (4.0) licence includes Attribution, so the licence is CC BY-NC. A student writing 'CC NC' has named a licence that does not exist.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Creative Commons license: the six current licences are CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC-ND

findings.claim: Flashcard 10 question: 'What replaced and extended RIPA in 2016?'
findings.truth: The Investigatory Powers Act 2016 repealed parts of RIPA (interception and communications-data acquisition) but RIPA Part II, covering directed and intrusive surveillance and covert human intelligence sources, remains in force. RIPA was not replaced. The lesson body correctly says 'supplemented', so the flashcard contradicts the content it revises.
findings.evidence: lesson 2 paragraph n24 ('later supplemented by the Investigatory Powers Act 2016'); Investigatory Powers Act 2016 repeal schedule

findings.claim: Both 8-mark mark schemes use a four-band ladder named Mastering (7-8) / Secure (5-6) / Developing (3-4) / Emerging (1-2).
findings.truth: House band vocabulary is Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band. Two options: (a) relabel here to Top band (7-8) / Upper-mid band (5-6) / Mid band (3-4) / Low band (1-2), or (b) leave both ladders to the fleet-wide band-ladder queue so every subject is relabelled to one shape at once. This unit is not special, so a one-off rewrite risks diverging from the canonical shape.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md band-name rule; the open band-ladder relabel queue in the retro fact-check programme
findings.ruling: NOTE: band ladders left for the programme-wide band-ladder sweep.

findings.claim: The Act created three principal offences (unauthorised access; access with intent; unauthorised modification).
findings.truth: True of the Act as passed in 1990, and the usual GCSE answer, so not an error. Two further offences were added later: section 3A, making or supplying articles for use in offences (2006), and section 3ZA, unauthorised acts causing serious damage, maximum life (2015). Section 3 was also renamed to 'unauthorised acts with intent to impair operation', though textbooks still say 'unauthorised modification'.
findings.evidence: Computer Misuse Act 1990 as amended by the Police and Justice Act 2006 and the Serious Crime Act 2015

findings.claim: The unit covers six Acts: DPA 2018, CMA 1990, CDPA 1988, Creative Commons, RIPA 2000, FOI Act 2000.
findings.truth: The spec legislation list has a seventh bullet, the Telecommunications Regulations Act 2000, which appears nowhere in the unit. The data protection principles are also not taught, only the individual rights. Both are content gaps rather than errors, so no edit, but a student could meet either in the exam.
findings.evidence: spec section 11 Legislation, bullet list (spec lines 899-907)

findings.claim: The 8-mark "Discuss Impacts" question is a regular feature of the exam.
findings.truth: The spec fixes only the paper facts: the theory paper is a 1 hour 45 minute written examination worth 100 marks and 50% of the qualification. It prints no question ladder and names no question type called 'Discuss Impacts'. The claim is unverifiable rather than impossible, so it is recorded, not edited.
findings.evidence: spec 2.1 assessment summary (spec lines 245-253); spec 3.1 AO weightings

findings.claim: toxic materials - including lead, mercury, cadmium and lithium - can leach into soil and groundwater
findings.truth: Lead, mercury and cadmium are the standard e-waste heavy metals and are correct. Lithium is mainly a fire and reactivity hazard in landfill rather than a classic leaching toxin, so it is the weakest of the four. Also note flashcard 5 answers 'Lead (also accept: mercury, cadmium, lithium).', which is a list-pattern answer that may fail the flashcard validator.
findings.evidence: standard e-waste hazardous-substance lists (lead, mercury, cadmium, brominated flame retardants)

findings.claim: The Data Protection Act 2018 / UK GDPR gives individuals four key rights
findings.truth: The UK GDPR gives eight rights (informed, access, rectification, erasure, restrict processing, portability, object, and rights over automated decision-making). The lesson names four of them and calls them 'key', which is not false, so no edit. A student should not read this as 'there are only four'.

summary: Both lessons carry findings. The two HIGH errors are a fabricated 2024 examiners' report claim in lesson 1 and a wrong legal classification in lesson 2 (Computer Misuse Act section 1 called a summary offence carrying 2 years, when it is triable either way with 2 years on indictment). Also fixed: an out-of-date data-centre electricity figure repeated four times, the Data Protection Act 2018 wrongly dated to after Brexit, the non-existent licence code 'CC NC', a flashcard saying the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 replaced RIPA, and board-style band names in student prose.
